overview: Memeware's Fly is a mode-dispatch module that runs most of its logic from a MovementEvent consumer, with one UpdateEvent handler for the Hypixel and Vanilla modes and an EventCollide handler for the Collision mode. The mode list spans eight strategies: a plain velocity-based Vanilla fly with an optional Anti-Kick ladder, a PvP Temple timer exploit, a Mineplex mode that places a block under the player and rides a build-up speed value that decays after a jump, a Hypixel micro-offset hover, an Old NCP sub-block y alternation, two Cubecraft modes that stream C18PacketSpectate packets and place held blocks, and a Collision mode that inflates the player's bounding box so no block can push the entity back. Every mode except Collision ends by zeroing motionY, so the server-side packet stream is the only thing the module changes.

sections.p: The module is three event handlers plus enable/disable state resets. eventConsumer0 listens to MovementEvent, which fires before the movement update is sent, and branches on the mode string; eventConsumer1 listens to UpdateEvent for the Hypixel and Vanilla modes; eventConsumer2 listens to EventCollide for the bounding-box override. onEnable records the starting position, resets the mineplexSpeed accumulator, the back toggle, the done flag and the down flag, and onDisable restores motionX/motionZ to 0.15, restores timer speed to 1.0 and re-sends the original held item slot for the Cubecraft modes. The constructor registers a Speed double from 0.1 to 5.0 and an Anti-Kick boolean that only the Vanilla mode reads.

The server-visible traffic is the interesting part. The Cubecraft modes call BlockUtil.placeHeldItemUnderPlayer, which places a block below the player, and surround that with two silent C09PacketHeldItemChange packets (to the block slot and back) plus a C18PacketSpectate with a hard-coded UUID; the spectate packet is sent every tick or every third tick depending on the mode, and the y jitter comes from the movement event rather than motion. The Mineplex mode alternates the move speed sign every tick while it builds up, increments mineplexSpeed by roughly 0.125 per two grounded ticks, then jumps with motionY 0.42 and switches to a decay phase where speed is multiplied by 0.979 per tick and motionY is nudged up by 0.039 or 0.032. The Old NCP mode alternates event y between -1.0E-9 and +1.0E-9 on every tick and pins motionY to zero, a classic sub-threshold float abuse.

The Vanilla mode drives motionY from the jump and sneak keys at half the speed setting, applies the speed setting through MovementUtils.setMoveSpeed, and when Anti-Kick is on and the 700ms Timer elapses it calls MovementUtils.fallPacket() and MovementUtils.ascendPacket(), which send the position packets that make a vanilla flying server re-validate the player. The PvP Temple mode sets timerSpeed to 0.6, applies 7.02 horizontal speed on every third tick and zero on the others, and on every tenth tick drops y by 1.0 then bounces it back by 1.0 the next tick. The Hypixel mode zeroes motionY and sets the update y to the current y plus 1.0E-9, adding another 1.0E-8 on even ticks. The Collision mode never touches packets: it replaces the collision box with a 4x2x4 box so the player cannot be pushed by entities or blocks.

files.label: Fly.java (module)
files.explanation:
The whole module is this one file. The MovementEvent consumer is the dispatch point: each mode branch mutates the event's y and horizontal speed, and the Cubecraft modes additionally emit C09 held-item swaps, block placements and C18 spectate packets through PacketUtil.sendPacketSilent. The UpdateEvent consumer handles Hypixel (micro-offset y) and Vanilla (motionY control plus the Anti-Kick fall/ascend ladder driven by the 700ms Timer). The Collision mode is an EventCollide handler that replaces the bounding box with a 4x2x4 box so the server's block collision cannot slow the player down.

The Cubecraft modes are worth a closer look. Cubecraft Slow, on every fourth tick, sets the event y to 0.00003 (or 1.0 when jumping) and otherwise applies base move speed with a -0.00001 descent, switching timerSpeed between 1.0 and 0.3 depending on the jump key and down to 0.1 when sneaking; the block placement under the player and the C18 spectate stream run every tick. Cubecraft Fast only places blocks on every third tick, applying 2.1 speed and a +0.0003 y spike on that tick and a -0.00015 y drift on the other two. Both modes end with motionY set to 0, so the vertical position is carried entirely by the event y and the block placements.

The remaining modes are simpler motion writes. Mineplex builds speed while grounded and then glides; Old NCP alternates ±1.0E-9 y; PvP Temple is the timer-speed plus 7.02 speed spike cycle with the y drop-and-bounce; Vanilla is the only mode that reads the Speed setting as a motion magnitude. onDisable cleans up by restoring move speed to 0.15 and timer speed to 1.0, and for the Cubecraft modes re-sends the original held item slot.

countering.label: SurvivalFly (movement physics envelope)
countering.explanation:
SurvivalFly rebuilds the allowed motion from the world instead of trusting the packet. The horizontal allowance comes from a speed estimation based on the player's sprint state and potion effects, and the vertical allowance comes from vDistRel, which initializes from the previous move's momentum and only accepts a few named envelopes: a zero-y move on ground, a jump, a step-up and a riptide launch. Crucially, the grounded state is derived from a block ray trace at the position, not from the packet's onGround flag, so claiming ground does not relax the envelope. A violation is (max(hDistanceAboveLimit, 0) + max(yDistanceAboveLimit, 0)) * 100 with a set-back.

The horizontal modes die first. PvP Temple's 7.02 blocks-per-tick spike on every third tick is roughly 20 times the ~0.31 sprint prediction, so hDistanceAboveLimit is around 6.7 and the violation is in the hundreds on the first spike, before the zero-speed ticks can average it down. Mineplex's build-up speed, which accumulates to the Speed setting times 1.3 before the jump, exceeds the envelope the same way, and the -1.0 y drop every 10 ticks in PvP Temple is a 1-block vertical move against an allowed descent of a few tenths, adding yDistanceAboveLimit on top. The Collision mode's inflated box does not help because NCP computes its own collision profile from the world data.

The vertical modes run into the same wall from the other side. Old NCP's ±1.0E-9 alternation and Hypixel's 1.0E-9 offsets are sub-pixel hover states: the envelope allows a zero-y move on ground, but in mid-air there is no momentum to inherit, so even a tiny y movement is judged against a near-zero allowance and the hover itself is a zero-y move in air that the envelope does not name. The Cubecraft modes' 0.00003 and -0.00015 drifts are similarly outside the airborne envelope. The Vanilla mode with Anti-Kick is the worst: MovementUtils.fallPacket and ascendPacket emit position packets that move several blocks at once, which present as multi-block vertical deltas the envelope cannot explain, producing immediate violations and set-backs on the first ladder cycle.

countering.label: Flight (hover, ascension, glide)
countering.explanation:
Arc v2's Flight checks the vertical profile of every move. The hover check fires when both the last and current vertical speeds are exactly 0.0 and airTicks passes maxHover, which is precisely the resting state of most Memeware modes: Old NCP, Hypixel and Cubecraft Fast all zero motionY while airborne, so the reported vertical speed is 0.0 tick after tick and the hover flag fires once the air-time threshold is crossed. The mode's sub-pixel y jitter does not rescue it, because the check compares the raw motion components and any nonzero value still fails the zero-y envelope the moment it is examined against gravity.

The ascension branch compares the rising vertical speed against the jump cap: vertical above maxHeight flags ascending_too_fast. PvP Temple's bounce-back of +1.0 per tick after the drop, Mineplex's 0.42 jump and the Vanilla mode's motionY of half the speed setting (up to 2.5 at the default 5.0 setting) all exceed the jump-derived cap on the first rising move. The descending branch applies the mirror logic: the vertical change must match a gravity-derived polynomial, and the module's abrupt -1.0 drop in PvP Temple and the instant 0 to 1.0 switches produce glide deltas that never match the expected curve, tripping the glide or descend flags.

Hawk's tolerance does not save any mode here. The horizontal-only drift modes still carry a vertical component that the check compares, and the Cubecraft modes' y values, while small, are nonzero in air where the expected value is a gravity-decayed fall, so the discrepancy accumulates. The Mineplex jump itself is the one legal vertical move in the whole module, but only for the single tick it lasts; the sustained flight around it is what Arc flags.

countering.label: Fly (predicted-velocity discrepancy)
countering.explanation:
Hawk's Fly runs a per-player vertical simulation. In air it predicts the next velocity as (previous estimated velocity - 0.08) * 0.98, the vanilla gravity step, and integrates it into an estimated position; the reported Y is compared against that estimate, and any discrepancy over the 0.0001 threshold is punished with a rubberband set-back. The sub-pixel modes are the direct targets: Old NCP's ±1.0E-9 alternation and Hypixel's 1.0E-9 offsets are so far below the predicted gravity decay of about 0.0784 blocks per tick that the estimate and the report diverge on the first tick, and the hover state, where motion is zero while airborne, diverges from the predicted fall within a tick or two.

PvP Temple's profile is even worse for the prediction model. The -1.0 drop followed by a +1.0 bounce every ten ticks produces a vertical trajectory that no gravity simulation produces, so the estimated position and the reported position separate by more than a block inside the cycle, well past the threshold. The Vanilla mode's motionY of half the speed setting ascends at up to 2.5 blocks per tick against a predicted fall, an instant discrepancy. When the client reports onGround, the check also requires the Y to fall between the previous Y and the estimated position, so the Anti-Kick ladder's position packets, which jump several blocks at once, land outside that window and trip the landing check.

The check's no-move tracking tolerates at most 20 ticks without a position update, so none of the modes can hide by suppressing movement packets. The Collision mode is the one strategy the vertical model does not see, because its bounding-box inflation produces ordinary movement; Hawk would still catch it on the horizontal prediction or the block-collision reconstruction, but the vertical Fly check itself is not what stops it.
